heading: PROPHET LŪṬ (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ)
title: COURAGE, DIGNITY & THE RIGHT CHOICE
themes: Tawḥīd • Moral Courage • Privacy • Trust • Safety • Personal Accountability
scope: 6 CONNECTED STORIES | 10 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 28 SELECTED AYĀT
introduction: This is the seventh ʿIBRAH Junior learning world in the Imaan & Akhlaq children’s curriculum. It follows the completed worlds on Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ and Ibrāhīm (peace be upon them). Prophet Lūṭ (AS) is introduced within the history of Prophetic guidance, and the content is anchored in revelation rather than invented historical dialogue. The compass motif from the previous world continues as a purely fictional contemporary learning device in Sheikh Uncle’s library.

The Qur’an presents Prophet Lūṭ’s mission, the grave sexual immorality and other wrongdoing among his people, their treatment of guests, his steadfast warning, the messengers’ instruction, rescue by Allah, and the decreed judgment. Younger readers need a careful, non-graphic mode of teaching without suppressing the theological meaning. The children’s fictional stories examine respect, safety, consent to share information, resistance to group pressure, and independent responsibility. Such everyday activities are educational applications, never a claim that a classroom joke is equivalent to the ancient people’s sins.

stories.title: The Compass and the Welcome Sign
stories.subtitle: A new name on the library shelf

blocks.text: Akhlaq had been checking the old compass every morning since the last journey. It sat in a velvet-lined case on Sheikh Uncle’s library desk, beside their notebook of lessons from Prophet Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him). The compass had no magical power. Sheikh Uncle had made that very clear. Still, its eleven tiny marks reminded the children of every question they had asked about truth, courage and trust in Allah.

That Saturday a different puzzle awaited them. A notice at the academy entrance read: WELCOME AND SAFETY WEEK — EVERY VISITOR DESERVES RESPECT. Below it was a list of volunteers. Imaan and Mohsina had been assigned to welcome a visiting reading group. Akhlaq and Mohsin were asked to prepare the hall.

‘Why do the girls get the important job?’ Akhlaq asked, lifting a box of chairs. ‘We are carrying furniture.’ Mohsina smiled. ‘Visitors might prefer chairs to a speech about how important you are.’ Mohsin laughed so loudly that he nearly dropped his end of the box.

When the guests arrived, a younger boy stood apart from the others. He seemed unsure where to go. Two students whispered about his unfamiliar accent. One of them mimicked the way he had said a word. The boy glanced at them and lowered his eyes. Imaan walked over, greeted him properly and showed him the reading corner. Akhlaq watched, suddenly understanding why the welcome sign mattered.

Later, Dadi Jaan visited the academy with Salaam. On the desk she noticed the compass and a new card placed beside it: THE STRONGEST DOOR IS NOT ALWAYS MADE OF WOOD. ‘Who wrote that?’ she asked. Sheikh Uncle raised an eyebrow. ‘Akhlaq.’ Dadi smiled. ‘An interesting beginning for our next Prophet’s story.’

She reminded the children that Prophet Lūṭ (peace be upon him) lived in a community whose serious wrongdoing had become widespread. He was sent by Allah to call his people away from evil and back to obedience. The Qur’an also teaches that Allah gave him judgment and knowledge, and rescued him from a town whose people practised evil (Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:74–75). ‘His message was not a story about an ordinary disagreement,’ Dadi explained. ‘It was a call to truth in the face of people who refused it.’

Akhlaq looked again at the boy in the reading corner. ‘So should we pretend a small unkind joke is the same as the wrongdoing of Lūṭ’s people?’ ‘No,’ Dadi replied firmly. ‘The Qur’anic account must stand on its own. But we can still learn not to join wrongdoing just because a crowd approves of it.’

When the visitors left, the younger boy returned to thank Imaan. ‘I almost asked to go home,’ he admitted. Akhlaq picked up the welcome card and turned it over. On the back, Sheikh Uncle had written the next clue: WHAT HAPPENS WHEN EVERYONE SAYS A WRONG THING IS NORMAL?
The first door of their new learning journey had opened without any magic at all.
Fictional story focus
Linked mission IDs
Age-appropriate ethical application
LUT-01

stories.title: Everyone Is Laughing
stories.subtitle: A message in the class group

blocks.text: Monday began with a class-group message that arrived before breakfast. Mohsin had forwarded a photograph of an untidy corner of the school hall. Someone had added a joke blaming the visiting reading group for the mess. Another student replied with laughing faces. Soon the picture was being shared again and again.

Imaan recognised the room. The corner had been untidy before the visitors arrived; she had helped move the boxes herself. She typed a reply explaining the mistake, then hesitated. The group was laughing. If she objected, would they begin laughing at her?

Akhlaq read over her shoulder. ‘We could just ignore it,’ he suggested. ‘It will disappear by tomorrow.’ Imaan shook her head. ‘The picture might disappear. The unfair accusation might not.’ She wrote one short message: That is not what happened. The boxes were already there. Please stop sharing this.

The response came quickly. ‘Relax, it’s only a joke.’ Another student added, ‘Everyone knows we are joking.’ Mohsina sent a message supporting Imaan. They told Sir Zameer privately and asked him to correct the accusation without publicly embarrassing the student who had first posted it.

That afternoon Sir Zameer placed two cards on the classroom board. One said, EVERYONE AGREES. The other said, IS IT RIGHT? ‘These are different questions,’ he told the class. ‘A mistake does not become good because people vote for it.’

He introduced a passage from Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt. Prophet Lūṭ’s people rejected his warning, and the Qur’an speaks not only of grave sexual immorality but also of wrongdoing on the roads and misconduct in their gatherings (29:28–29). ‘This is a serious historical account of rejection and divine judgment,’ he said. ‘Our class chat is not its equivalent. But the habit of treating wrong as entertainment is something a learner should recognise and resist.’

One student asked whether that meant people could insult anyone they thought had done wrong. ‘Absolutely not,’ Sir Zameer replied. ‘A Muslim is accountable for personal speech and conduct. We do not turn a Qur’anic lesson into permission to threaten, humiliate, expose or harm another person. We must learn the guidance, act rightly ourselves, and treat people with dignity.’

After class, Mohsin approached the visitor who had been wrongly blamed. ‘I should have checked before forwarding that,’ he said. ‘I’m sorry.’ He helped Sir Zameer remove the misleading message and replace it with an accurate note. It was not easy, but it was better than defending a mistake with more jokes.

At home, Akhlaq wrote on the second card in their compass notebook: A CROWD CAN MAKE NOISE. IT CANNOT MAKE WRONG RIGHT. Then he noticed that Sheikh Uncle had left a third card tucked inside: IF SOMEONE KNOCKS ON YOUR DOOR, WHAT DO YOU OWE THEM?
‘A chair?’ he guessed. Imaan smiled. ‘Maybe something more important.’

stories.title: A Visitor at the Gate
stories.subtitle: A family learns what safety means

blocks.text: The guests for Friday evening were a family newly settled in the neighbourhood. Salamah had asked Imaan and Akhlaq to help prepare the sitting room. Imaan arranged drinking water; Akhlaq straightened the cushions three times, then proudly placed his best drawing on the wall. Mohsina and Mohsin arrived early to help set the table.

Half an hour before the visit, Akhlaq noticed a small message in a school chat asking where the family lived. ‘I know!’ he exclaimed. ‘They told Abbu their address. I can send the location.’ Imaan stopped him. ‘They gave that information to Abbu for a reason. It is not ours to circulate.’
‘But I am trying to help,’ Akhlaq protested. Mohsina lifted the welcome sign from last week. ‘Helping people includes respecting the information they trust you with.’ Akhlaq put away his phone.

When the doorbell rang, Salaam greeted the family. The youngest child was shy, and Imaan brought out a simple board game without asking uncomfortable questions. The adults talked quietly. It seemed such an ordinary evening that Akhlaq wondered why Dadi Jaan had called it their third lesson.

After the guests departed, Dadi opened the Qur’an to Sūrat Hūd. She explained that the Qur’an describes visitors coming to Prophet Lūṭ (peace be upon him). He was distressed because he knew of the danger posed by the wrongdoing of his people (11:77). In the account, a hostile crowd came toward the guests and Lūṭ called for reverence of Allah and protection of his guests (11:78). The people’s actions were not harmless curiosity. They were a serious violation of decency and the rights of others.

‘Did the visitors need him to perform a clever trick?’ Akhlaq asked. ‘The lesson is not about finding a game solution to an assault,’ Dadi answered. ‘It is about recognising the wrong clearly. The guests were entitled to protection, and Allah’s decree would unfold. We will not invent the words or actions that revelation does not report.’

Dadi then brought the lesson back to their home. Guests deserved a welcome, but they also deserved privacy. Children should not share a guest’s address, photographs or personal information without permission. If a visitor faced threats, children should not try to confront dangerous adults; they should seek help immediately from responsible adults and emergency services as needed.

Akhlaq looked at his phone. He could still see the unfinished message containing the family’s address. He deleted it. ‘That was a near miss,’ he admitted. ‘You stopped before causing harm,’ Salaam replied. ‘That matters too.’

Imaan looked at the compass notebook. She added a sentence below the third card: A SAFE WELCOME MEANS MORE THAN OPENING THE DOOR. Then Dadi Jaan quietly turned the page and asked, ‘What if someone who knows your household also ignores the truth?’

Age-appropriate ethical application

stories.title: The Secret That Was Not Ours
stories.subtitle: The difference between belonging and responsibility

blocks.text: A surprise reading exhibition was being planned at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy. Each class was preparing a display, but the date had not yet been announced. The teachers wanted everyone to be ready together. Akhlaq knew the date because he was helping Sir Zameer with the printed notices.

During recess, his friend Hamza asked when the exhibition would take place. ‘I could tell you,’ Akhlaq said, enjoying the importance of being trusted with information. Hamza promised not to repeat it. The temptation was immediate: it would feel good to be the one person who knew.
Imaan was sitting nearby. ‘Is it yours to share?’ she asked. Akhlaq sighed. ‘You always make information sound like a responsibility.’ ‘Sometimes it is,’ she answered.

That evening Salamah placed three cards on the table: FAMILY, FRIENDSHIP, and CHOICE. ‘Which of these tells Allah what choice you must make?’ she asked. Mohsin guessed family. Mohsina chose friendship, then changed her mind. Imaan pointed at the last card. ‘Each person still answers for their own actions.’

Salamah opened Sūrat al-Taḥrīm 66:10. Allah gives the wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ as examples of people whose close connection to righteous Prophets did not benefit them when they rejected faith. ‘The word betrayal here must be taught carefully,’ she said. ‘Ibn Kathīr explains that it concerns betrayal in faith, not adultery. We must never accuse a Prophet’s wife of sexual misconduct.’

Akhlaq raised his hand as if they were in class. ‘Then why are we learning this with my secret exhibition date?’ Salamah smiled. ‘They are not equivalent situations. Your secret is a small, modern responsibility. The Qur’an teaches something far greater: closeness to good people does not replace personal belief or accountability. Nobody becomes righteous simply because of their surname or friends.’

The next morning Hamza asked again. Akhlaq replied that Sir Zameer would announce the exhibition soon. Hamza was disappointed. ‘You have become very careful.’ ‘I was given a task,’ Akhlaq said. ‘I want to do it properly.’ Instead of sharing the date, he offered to help Hamza finish his book display.

The announcement arrived that afternoon, just as promised. Hamza smiled at Akhlaq and admitted that waiting had not harmed him. Akhlaq looked at the notebook and wrote: GOOD COMPANY HELPS ME. IT DOES NOT MAKE MY CHOICES FOR ME.
That night a fifth card appeared beneath the compass. It read: SOME DOORS SHOULD BE LEFT BEHIND. For the first time, the clue did not sound like a mystery. It sounded like a warning to act wisely.

stories.title: The Door We Walked Away From
stories.subtitle: Courage sometimes means seeking help

blocks.text: On Thursday afternoon the children were rehearsing for the academy exhibition. A group of older students began gathering near the back entrance. They laughed when younger students walked past and blocked the corridor to make them squeeze through. One boy told Mohsin to leave his display materials on the floor and come back later.

Mohsin was tempted to push past them. He was strong enough to do it, and he remembered the strength competition from Prophet Hūd’s volume. But he also remembered how easily a desire to win could make people careless. He took a step backwards.

‘We should tell Sir Zameer,’ Imaan said. ‘They will call us scared,’ Akhlaq replied. ‘Safety is more important than their opinion,’ Mohsina answered. They walked together to the office, informed an adult, and waited in a supervised room while staff addressed the situation. Nobody was asked to become a hero by risking injury.

Later, Dadi Jaan explained the closing part of Prophet Lūṭ’s account. After the people persisted in wrongdoing, the messengers brought news of Allah’s decree. Lūṭ and those with him who were to be saved were told to depart by night (Hūd 11:81; al-Ḥijr 15:65). His wife was excepted from the rescue according to the revealed account. The rescue was by Allah’s mercy; the punishment came through Allah’s command.

‘Was Lūṭ running away because he was cowardly?’ Akhlaq asked. Dadi shook her head. ‘He had faithfully delivered the message. Obeying Allah’s command to leave was not cowardice. A believer does not have to remain in a dangerous place to prove courage. And children must never think they have to confront attackers alone.’

Mohsin sat quietly for a moment. ‘I wanted to make those older boys move myself.’ Salaam nodded. ‘You chose a safer path. You also helped protect other students who might have faced the same problem. That is responsible courage.’

Imaan asked another question: ‘If a family has one person who disagrees, does that mean we can decide they are bad?’ Dadi answered carefully. ‘No. We cannot claim to know another person’s ultimate standing before Allah. The Qur’an tells us what occurred in a particular revealed account. We must not use it to accuse an ordinary family member or say that a child’s relatives determine the child’s worth.’

The following morning the school changed its visitor route, posted staff at the corridor and gave younger students a safe contact point. The children saw that protection often depended on calm reporting and responsible adults working together.

When Akhlaq opened the compass case, the fifth card had a new sentence on its back: LEAVING DANGER CAN BE AN ACT OF WISDOM. He placed it carefully beside the others. The final card was not in the case. It was waiting in a book of maps.

stories.title: The Map with No Invented City
stories.subtitle: What we can learn without pretending to know

blocks.text: Sheikh Uncle covered the library table with maps, a large Qur’an stand, and three small labels. One label read REVELATION. Another read REPORTED EXPLANATION. The third read WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW. The children were preparing an exhibition on the lessons of Prophet Lūṭ (peace be upon him), and their final challenge was to place information under the correct heading.

Akhlaq reached for a colourful map labelled EXACT CITY OF LŪṬ. It included a bright red dot and a dramatic picture of a ruined street. ‘This would look exciting,’ he said. Sheikh Uncle leaned forward. ‘But can we prove every detail on it?’ Akhlaq examined the small print. ‘No source is named.’ ‘Then excitement is not enough,’ Sheikh Uncle replied.

Imaan chose a different card: Allah rescued Lūṭ and the believers and destroyed the wrongdoers by His decree. ‘Revelation,’ she said, pointing to passages including al-ʿAnkabūt 29:32–35 and Hūd 11:81–83. Mohsina selected another: An identifiable sign was left for people who use reason (29:35). She placed that under REVELATION as well. Mohsin selected a card that said, We can accurately identify every guest by name. He placed it in WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW.

Then Dadi Jaan came to hear their presentations. Akhlaq spoke first. He explained that Prophet Lūṭ had called his people to righteousness and warned against serious sexual immorality and other public wrongdoing. He did not pretend that the story was merely about hospitality. ‘The Qur’an is clear about moral limits,’ he said, ‘and we also have to be clear that no one is permitted to bully or harm another person because of our lesson.’

Imaan continued with the account of the guests, the people’s hostility, the command to depart, and Allah’s rescue and judgment. She did not use frightening images or claim to know what revelation had not told them. Mohsina explained that the children’s classroom stories were modern fictional applications; they were not scenes from the Prophet’s life. Mohsin closed by saying that defending privacy, resisting harmful pressure and seeking adult help were useful habits for their daily lives.

One younger visitor listened to the exhibition and then raised his hand. ‘Does Allah punish every place where something bad happens?’ Sheikh Uncle answered gently, ‘No one may look at an ordinary disaster or illness and claim to know Allah’s hidden judgment. We learn the particular judgment Allah revealed about this people, and we leave the unseen to Him.’

The exhibition ended without a dramatic light, a spinning needle, or a sudden door. But Akhlaq did not mind. He placed the last card beside the compass. It read: KNOW THE TRUTH. TREAT PEOPLE WITH DIGNITY. ACT RESPONSIBLY.

On the way home, Imaan asked what journey would come next. Sheikh Uncle smiled. ‘Remember the family of Ibrāhīm? There are still lessons of promise, trust and responsibility that we have not studied.’ Akhlaq tucked the compass case into his bag. This time he did not shake it to find another secret mark. He opened his notebook instead.
The journey would continue through learning, not through inventing history.

missions.title: The Messenger and the Message

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Tawḥīd, Prophethood, courage | Virtue to practice: Respect the truth
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 21:74
وَلوطًا ءاتَينـٰهُ حُكمًا وَعِلمًا وَنَجَّينـٰهُ مِنَ القَريَةِ الَّتى كانَت تَعمَلُ الخَبـٰئِثَ ۗ إِنَّهُم كانوا قَومَ سَوءٍ فـٰسِقينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: Allah granted Lūṭ sound judgment and knowledge and rescued him from a town committing wicked deeds.
Understand the revealed lesson

Allah presents Lūṭ as a Prophet and among the messengers. The Qur’an says that Allah granted him sound judgment and knowledge and rescued him from a town engaged in wicked deeds. His mission must be understood as a call to obedience to Allah, not just an example of a courageous individual disagreeing with neighbours. The inhabitants’ response was part of a serious religious and moral rejection. Being in a small minority did not change the truth of the message he conveyed.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge

A new child in your study group answers a difficult question correctly, but several classmates refuse to listen because he is younger. Imaan asks everyone to check the answer instead of judging the speaker.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Ignore the correct answer because the class majority disagrees.
choices.feedback: A large group can be mistaken. Revisit the explanation and examine what is true.

choices.text: Listen carefully, check the evidence, and speak respectfully.
choices.feedback: Truth should be examined fairly; age, popularity, and group approval do not replace evidence.

choices.text: Tell the younger child to stop asking questions.
choices.feedback: Silencing someone because they are younger does not show fairness or humility.

missions.action: Listen carefully to one person you usually overlook, then respond respectfully to what they actually say.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: When have I confused popularity with truth?

missions.title: When Wrongdoing Becomes Familiar

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Moral boundaries and self-control | Virtue to practice: Choose right over popularity
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 7:80
وَلوطًا إِذ قالَ لِقَومِهِ أَتَأتونَ الفـٰحِشَةَ ما سَبَقَكُم بِها مِن أَحَدٍ مِنَ العـٰلَمينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: Lūṭ rebuked his people for a grave indecency not previously committed by anyone among the worlds.
Understand the revealed lesson

The Qur’an records Lūṭ’s rebuke of grave sexual immorality among men; the account cannot be reduced to ordinary rudeness or merely to disliking strangers. For older children, a calm, non-graphic explanation may identify the sexual conduct condemned in these verses according to classical Islamic teaching. For younger children, a trusted adult should explain that Allah commands moral boundaries and protects dignity without graphic description. The activity that follows is a separate, small-scale example of refusing a wrong action—not an equivalence with the ancient people’s transgression.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Several classmates want to use someone’s private photograph as a joke. Akhlaq knows they have no permission and that the image may embarrass the person.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Share it because many people have already seen it.
choices.feedback: Repeated sharing increases harm; it does not make sharing acceptable.

choices.text: Refuse to share it and ask a responsible adult for help stopping the spread.
choices.feedback: Popularity does not turn disrespect into permission. Protecting others’ privacy is a wise modern application.

choices.text: Add an even more hurtful caption.
choices.feedback: Humiliating someone adds to harm and turns a wrong choice into another one.

missions.action: Before sharing a photo or message today, check whether you have permission; if not, do not share it.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: Can I say no without insulting the people asking me?

missions.title: When the Street Is No Longer Safe

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Public wrongdoing, rights of others | Virtue to practice: Protect the vulnerable
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 29:29
أَئِنَّكُم لَتَأتونَ الرِّجالَ وَتَقطَعونَ السَّبيلَ وَتَأتونَ فى ناديكُمُ المُنكَرَ ۖ فَما كانَ جَوابَ قَومِهِ إِلّا أَن قالُوا ائتِنا بِعَذابِ اللَّهِ إِن كُنتَ مِنَ الصّـٰدِقينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: He condemned their sexual misconduct with men, their interruption of roads, and evil behavior in gatherings; they rejected his warning.
Understand the revealed lesson

Alongside its condemnation of grave sexual misconduct, al-ʿAnkabūt 29:29 rebukes the people for disrupting roads and committing evil in their gatherings. Tafsir reports describe aggression toward travelers and shameless behavior in public. This is not a description of ordinary disagreement; it is a warning about a community that defended wrongdoing. Our daily-life lesson is to take other people’s safety seriously and seek proper help when someone is intimidated.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
A group of older students blocks the corridor to frighten younger pupils. Mohsin feels angry and wants to push through them to make a point.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Fight them to prove you are brave.
choices.feedback: A physical fight may put you or others in danger. Safety comes first.

choices.text: Move to a safe place and report the obstruction to a trusted adult.
choices.feedback: Protecting safety through responsible adults is courage with wisdom; a child need not confront threatening people.

choices.text: Take a video to mock the younger pupils later.
choices.feedback: Recording or mocking frightened children fails to protect them and may expose them further.

missions.action: Notice one shared space today and help keep it safe and accessible for others.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: What is the difference between courage and reckless confrontation?

missions.title: The Call That Was Rejected

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Sincere responsibility, supplication | Virtue to practice: Speak truth without abuse
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 26:164
وَما أَسـَٔلُكُم عَلَيهِ مِن أَجرٍ ۖ إِن أَجرِىَ إِلّا عَلىٰ رَبِّ العـٰلَمينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: He said he asked for no payment for conveying the message; his reward was with Allah.
Understand the revealed lesson

Prophet Lūṭ made clear that he was not asking his people for payment, and his opponents threatened to expel him. The Qur’an also preserves his supplication for help against corruption. His resolve belonged to Prophetic obedience to Allah, not stubbornness for its own sake. Children can practise telling the truth respectfully while remembering that threatening or intimidating situations require trusted-adult intervention. They must not imitate a Prophet by confronting dangerous crowds alone.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Akhlaq tells his friends that an accusation about a visitor is false. Some laugh and threaten to exclude him from their team.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Repeat the false accusation so they will include you.
choices.feedback: Trading truth for inclusion hurts the person being falsely accused.

choices.text: State the facts calmly and ask the teacher to address the issue.
choices.feedback: Explain what is true without humiliation. Asking for help is a responsible response to exclusion or intimidation.

choices.text: Call them cruel names until they stop.
choices.feedback: Insults can turn a needed correction into more harm.

missions.action: Correct one small false statement kindly, using words that do not humiliate anyone.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: How do I stay truthful without becoming harsh?

missions.title: The Guests Were a Trust

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Hospitality, privacy, protection | Virtue to practice: Respect guests
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 11:77
وَلَمّا جاءَت رُسُلُنا لوطًا سىءَ بِهِم وَضاقَ بِهِم ذَرعًا وَقالَ هـٰذا يَومٌ عَصيبٌ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: The messengers came to Lūṭ; he was deeply distressed by concern for the danger surrounding his visitors.
Understand the revealed lesson

Sūrat Hūd tells how messengers came to Lūṭ and he felt distressed because he understood the danger around him. A hostile crowd approached, and he appealed to them to fear Allah and not disgrace him with regard to his guests. Editors must explain the complete verse and its classical discussion rather than presenting its reference to his ‘daughters’ in isolation. The main lesson for young children is not to dramatize the guests’ danger but to understand that people have rights and their safety cannot be treated as entertainment.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
During a family visit, Hamza asks Akhlaq to send him a guest’s home address. The guest shared it privately with Salaam to arrange the visit.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Send the address to be helpful.
choices.feedback: Good intentions do not give permission to disclose another person’s address.

choices.text: Keep the address private and ask the guest or adult before sharing any information.
choices.feedback: A respectful welcome includes consent, privacy, and thoughtful protection of other people’s information.

choices.text: Guess the address and send that instead.
choices.feedback: Sharing guessed personal information is also careless and may create risk.

missions.action: Ask permission before taking or sharing a visitor’s photograph or personal details today.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: What would make a guest feel safe and respected in our home?

missions.title: When a Crowd Pressed the Door

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Limits of force, seeking protection | Virtue to practice: Choose safe help
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 11:79
قالوا لَقَد عَلِمتَ ما لَنا فى بَناتِكَ مِن حَقٍّ وَإِنَّكَ لَتَعلَمُ ما نُريدُ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: The people answered that they did not seek what Lūṭ was urging and insisted on their own desire.
Understand the revealed lesson

The hostile crowd in Sūrat Hūd refused Lūṭ’s appeal and threatened the safety of the visitors. Lūṭ expressed distress at his lack of human power to restrain them. It would be wrong to turn this terrible episode into a chase game, a combat puzzle, or a challenge in which a child ‘saves the Prophet.’ The children’s separate scenario teaches the practical right to seek help, leave dangerous spaces, and ask adults to protect those at risk.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Two older children are aggressively demanding that a younger visitor give them his bag. Imaan and Mohsina see it from a distance.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Run between them and fight for the bag.
choices.feedback: Trying to fight larger aggressors can put everyone at greater risk.

choices.text: Move to safety together and immediately alert a responsible adult.
choices.feedback: In a threatening situation, use a safe path and involve trusted adults promptly.

choices.text: Stay nearby filming the confrontation.
choices.feedback: Filming instead of helping may expose the victim and delay protection.

missions.action: Identify one trustworthy adult you can go to for help if a child is threatened.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: Who can help me when I cannot solve danger alone?

missions.title: Accountable for My Own Choice

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Belief, responsibility, family | Virtue to practice: Own your decisions
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 66:10

ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا لِلَّذينَ كَفَرُوا امرَأَتَ نوحٍ وَامرَأَتَ لوطٍ ۖ كانَتا تَحتَ عَبدَينِ مِن عِبادِنا صـٰلِحَينِ فَخانَتاهُما فَلَم يُغنِيا عَنهُما مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيـًٔا وَقيلَ ادخُلَا النّارَ مَعَ الدّٰخِلينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: Allah uses the wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ as examples of people who betrayed faith while close to two righteous servants; closeness did not replace belief.
Understand the revealed lesson

Allah’s example in al-Taḥrīm 66:10 makes an essential point: being close to a Prophet does not replace personal faith. Classical Tafsir, including Ibn Kathīr, explicitly rejects interpreting the wife’s betrayal as adultery; it refers to disbelief and religious opposition. Children must not turn this into suspicion about family members. The modern school-story analogy is narrower: friends and family can influence us, but they do not make our choices for us. Respectful treatment of relatives remains obligatory.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Akhlaq knows the exhibition announcement date because the teacher trusted him to prepare notices. His friend wants him to reveal it secretly.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Tell the secret to keep the friend happy.
choices.feedback: A friend’s wish does not cancel a responsibility you accepted.

choices.text: Explain kindly that the information belongs to the teacher to announce.
choices.feedback: Friendship can continue without crossing a reasonable trust. Your own choice matters.

choices.text: Invent a false date to confuse the friend.
choices.feedback: Inventing a lie adds a second wrong to the first temptation.

missions.action: Keep one small commitment or confidence you have been trusted with today.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: Am I choosing what is right or merely following someone close to me?

missions.title: A Wise Departure

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Responding to guidance, safety | Virtue to practice: Know when to seek safety
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 11:81

قالوا يـٰلوطُ إِنّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ لَن يَصِلوا إِلَيكَ ۖ فَأَسرِ بِأَهلِكَ بِقِطعٍ مِنَ الَّيلِ وَلا يَلتَفِت مِنكُم أَحَدٌ إِلَّا امرَأَتَكَ ۖ إِنَّهُ مُصيبُها ما أَصابَهُم ۚ إِنَّ مَوعِدَهُمُ الصُّبحُ ۚ أَلَيسَ الصُّبحُ بِقَريبٍ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: The messengers declared their mission, reassured Lūṭ, and instructed him about departure and those excepted from rescue.
Understand the revealed lesson

The messengers instructed Lūṭ concerning departure by night and the rescue that Allah had decreed. This was a specific command in a specific revealed history. We must not suggest that children should run away from home or treat ordinary disagreement as a Prophetic migration. The practical, separate skill is learning to recognize threatening circumstances, follow a safe emergency plan, and seek responsible adult assistance rather than escalating danger.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Older pupils are blocking the hall and taunting younger children. Mohsin wants to confront them, but Sir Zameer’s office is nearby.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Start a shouting argument.
choices.feedback: Confrontation may increase danger and is not required of a child.

choices.text: Leave the unsafe area and report it to Sir Zameer with the younger students.
choices.feedback: Wise courage sometimes means leaving danger and using trustworthy support.

choices.text: Tell everyone to be quiet and stay where they are until the older pupils leave.
choices.feedback: Staying in an unsafe space when help is available is not a duty.

missions.action: With a caregiver, identify the safest adult-help point at home or school.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: Why can leaving danger be responsible rather than cowardly?

missions.title: Mercy, Rescue, and Judgment

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Divine judgment, mercy, humility | Virtue to practice: Avoid careless judgments
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 29:32
قالَ إِنَّ فيها لوطًا ۚ قالوا نَحنُ أَعلَمُ بِمَن فيها ۖ لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ وَأَهلَهُ إِلَّا امرَأَتَهُ كانَت مِنَ الغـٰبِرينَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: Ibrāhīm expressed concern about Lūṭ; the messengers stated Allah knew who was there and would save him and his family except his wife.
Understand the revealed lesson

The Qur’an records that Allah rescued Lūṭ and those whom He willed to save, while the rejecting wrongdoers were overtaken by the decreed punishment. The text should be taught as real divine judgment, not reinterpreted as a mere natural inconvenience. At the same time, children must never be encouraged to label a living person, a family’s hardship, a flood, an earthquake, or a community’s disaster as a known act of Allah’s punishment. Only revelation establishes the particular judgment described here.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge
Someone posts that a family’s damaged house is proof that Allah is angry with them. Imaan knows nobody has revelation about that family.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Forward the message to warn others.
choices.feedback: Sharing unverified claims about divine judgment harms people and claims knowledge you do not have.

choices.text: Reject the ungrounded claim and offer the family practical kindness.
choices.feedback: We cannot claim knowledge of Allah’s unseen judgment about an ordinary person; kindness and accuracy are required.

choices.text: Use the claim to make fun of the family.
choices.feedback: Mocking people in hardship is cruel and has no basis in our lesson.

missions.action: Offer one simple kindness to someone facing difficulty, without asking them to explain their hardship.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: How can I believe in divine justice while avoiding guesses about others?

missions.title: An Honest Map of the Past

discover.label: Core theme
discover.text: Evidence literacy, reflection, dignity | Virtue to practice: Tell history faithfully
Discover & read
FIRST ANCHOR — QURʾĀN 29:35
وَلَقَد تَرَكنا مِنها ءايَةً بَيِّنَةً لِقَومٍ يَعقِلونَ

discover.label: Working meaning
discover.text: Allah said a clear sign had been left for those who use reason.
Understand the revealed lesson

Allah says that an evident sign was left for people who use reason, and Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt remembers the rescue of Lūṭ and the fate of the others. Children must understand that the purpose is reflection upon revelation and obedience, not a tourist hunt for the exact site of judgment or dramatic invented geography. Distinguish what the Qur’an establishes from later identifications and speculation. The central truth includes grave immorality, rejecting a Prophet, hostility toward guests, rescue and divine punishment; the modern educational applications remain separate and limited.
A moment to reflect

The truth of the Qur’anic account does not depend on whether a crowd accepted the Messenger. We learn from revealed history and then carefully ask what responsible, kind, truthful action is required in a different modern situation.
Decide — a separate fictional challenge

Team Amanah is preparing a classroom poster. A bright picture names an exact ancient street and shows details nobody can verify. Another poster uses Qur’anic references and clearly labels uncertainties.

missions.question: What should Imaan or Akhlaq do?

choices.text: Choose the dramatic poster without checking because it is exciting.
choices.feedback: A dramatic picture is not evidence that its details are historically reliable.

choices.text: Use the accurate poster and label any uncertain details honestly.
choices.feedback: Truthful learning does not need invented scenery. Show exactly what revelation supports.

choices.text: Invent extra details so the other poster looks more impressive.
choices.feedback: Invented details mislead other learners about sacred history.

missions.action: Check one religious or historical claim against a reliable source before repeating it.

remember.label: Reflection question
remember.text: Why does saying “I do not know” sometimes show more knowledge?

review.arabic: وَلوطًا إِذ قالَ لِقَومِهِ أَتَأتونَ الفـٰحِشَةَ ما سَبَقَكُم بِها مِن أَحَدٍ مِنَ العـٰلَمينَ
review.meaning: Lūṭ rebuked his people for a grave indecency not previously committed by anyone among the worlds.

review.arabic: إِنَّكُم لَتَأتونَ الرِّجالَ شَهوَةً مِن دونِ النِّساءِ ۚ بَل أَنتُم قَومٌ مُسرِفونَ
review.meaning: He condemned their lustful approach to men instead of women and described the people as transgressors.

review.arabic: وَلَمّا جاءَت رُسُلُنا لوطًا سىءَ بِهِم وَضاقَ بِهِم ذَرعًا وَقالَ هـٰذا يَومٌ عَصيبٌ
review.meaning: The messengers came to Lūṭ; he was deeply distressed by concern for the danger surrounding his visitors.

review.arabic: وَجاءَهُ قَومُهُ يُهرَعونَ إِلَيهِ وَمِن قَبلُ كانوا يَعمَلونَ السَّيِّـٔاتِ ۚ قالَ يـٰقَومِ هـٰؤُلاءِ بَناتى هُنَّ أَطهَرُ لَكُم ۖ فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَلا تُخزونِ فى ضَيفى ۖ أَلَيسَ مِنكُم رَجُلٌ رَشيدٌ
review.meaning: His people rushed toward his guests; he urged them to fear Allah and not disgrace him with regard to the guests. The full verse requires classical commentary on its wording about daughters.

review.arabic: قالوا لَقَد عَلِمتَ ما لَنا فى بَناتِكَ مِن حَقٍّ وَإِنَّكَ لَتَعلَمُ ما نُريدُ
review.meaning: The people answered that they did not seek what Lūṭ was urging and insisted on their own desire.

review.arabic: قالَ لَو أَنَّ لى بِكُم قُوَّةً أَو ءاوى إِلىٰ رُكنٍ شَديدٍ
review.meaning: Lūṭ expressed his distress, wishing for strength or reliable support against the wrongdoing.

review.arabic: قالوا يـٰلوطُ إِنّا رُسُلُ رَبِّكَ لَن يَصِلوا إِلَيكَ ۖ فَأَسرِ بِأَهلِكَ بِقِطعٍ مِنَ الَّيلِ وَلا يَلتَفِت مِنكُم أَحَدٌ إِلَّا امرَأَتَكَ ۖ إِنَّهُ مُصيبُها ما أَصابَهُم ۚ إِنَّ مَوعِدَهُمُ الصُّبحُ ۚ أَلَيسَ الصُّبحُ بِقَريبٍ
review.meaning: The messengers declared their mission, reassured Lūṭ, and instructed him about departure and those excepted from rescue.

review.arabic: فَلَمّا جاءَ أَمرُنا جَعَلنا عـٰلِيَها سافِلَها وَأَمطَرنا عَلَيها حِجارَةً مِن سِجّيلٍ مَنضودٍ
review.meaning: The Qur’an recounts the divine judgment that overtook the wrongdoers.

review.arabic: مُسَوَّمَةً عِندَ رَبِّكَ ۖ وَما هِىَ مِنَ الظّـٰلِمينَ بِبَعيدٍ
review.meaning: The punishment was marked by Allah and is a warning in its revealed context.

review.arabic: فَأَسرِ بِأَهلِكَ بِقِطعٍ مِنَ الَّيلِ وَاتَّبِع أَدبـٰرَهُم وَلا يَلتَفِت مِنكُم أَحَدٌ وَامضوا حَيثُ تُؤمَرونَ
review.meaning: Lūṭ was told to travel with his family by night and follow the command concerning departure.

review.arabic: وَلوطًا ءاتَينـٰهُ حُكمًا وَعِلمًا وَنَجَّينـٰهُ مِنَ القَريَةِ الَّتى كانَت تَعمَلُ الخَبـٰئِثَ ۗ إِنَّهُم كانوا قَومَ سَوءٍ فـٰسِقينَ
review.meaning: Allah granted Lūṭ sound judgment and knowledge and rescued him from a town committing wicked deeds.

review.arabic: وَأَدخَلنـٰهُ فى رَحمَتِنا ۖ إِنَّهُ مِنَ الصّـٰلِحينَ
review.meaning: Allah admitted Lūṭ to His mercy and names him among the righteous.

review.arabic: كَذَّبَت قَومُ لوطٍ المُرسَلينَ
review.meaning: The people of Lūṭ rejected the messengers.

review.arabic: إِذ قالَ لَهُم أَخوهُم لوطٌ أَلا تَتَّقونَ
review.meaning: Lūṭ addressed his people as their brother and asked them to be mindful of Allah.

review.arabic: إِنّى لَكُم رَسولٌ أَمينٌ
review.meaning: He identified himself as a trustworthy messenger.

review.arabic: فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطيعونِ
review.meaning: He told his people to be mindful of Allah and obey the messenger.

review.arabic: وَما أَسـَٔلُكُم عَلَيهِ مِن أَجرٍ ۖ إِن أَجرِىَ إِلّا عَلىٰ رَبِّ العـٰلَمينَ
review.meaning: He said he asked for no payment for conveying the message; his reward was with Allah.

review.arabic: قالوا لَئِن لَم تَنتَهِ يـٰلوطُ لَتَكونَنَّ مِنَ المُخرَجينَ
review.meaning: The opponents threatened Lūṭ with expulsion.

review.arabic: وَلوطًا إِذ قالَ لِقَومِهِ إِنَّكُم لَتَأتونَ الفـٰحِشَةَ ما سَبَقَكُم بِها مِن أَحَدٍ مِنَ العـٰلَمينَ
review.meaning: Lūṭ rebuked his people for a grave indecency.

review.arabic: أَئِنَّكُم لَتَأتونَ الرِّجالَ وَتَقطَعونَ السَّبيلَ وَتَأتونَ فى ناديكُمُ المُنكَرَ ۖ فَما كانَ جَوابَ قَومِهِ إِلّا أَن قالُوا ائتِنا بِعَذابِ اللَّهِ إِن كُنتَ مِنَ الصّـٰدِقينَ
review.meaning: He condemned their sexual misconduct with men, their interruption of roads, and evil behavior in gatherings; they rejected his warning.

review.arabic: قالَ رَبِّ انصُرنى عَلَى القَومِ المُفسِدينَ
review.meaning: Lūṭ prayed to Allah for help against the corrupt people.

review.arabic: قالَ إِنَّ فيها لوطًا ۚ قالوا نَحنُ أَعلَمُ بِمَن فيها ۖ لَنُنَجِّيَنَّهُ وَأَهلَهُ إِلَّا امرَأَتَهُ كانَت مِنَ الغـٰبِرينَ
review.meaning: Ibrāhīm expressed concern about Lūṭ; the messengers stated Allah knew who was there and would save him and his family except his wife.

review.arabic: وَلَمّا أَن جاءَت رُسُلُنا لوطًا سىءَ بِهِم وَضاقَ بِهِم ذَرعًا وَقالوا لا تَخَف وَلا تَحزَن ۖ إِنّا مُنَجّوكَ وَأَهلَكَ إِلَّا امرَأَتَكَ كانَت مِنَ الغـٰبِرينَ
review.meaning: The messengers came to Lūṭ, reassured him, and repeated the news of rescue by Allah’s decree.

review.arabic: وَلَقَد تَرَكنا مِنها ءايَةً بَيِّنَةً لِقَومٍ يَعقِلونَ
review.meaning: Allah said a clear sign had been left for those who use reason.

review.arabic: وَإِنَّ لوطًا لَمِنَ المُرسَلينَ
review.meaning: The Qur’an affirms that Lūṭ was among the messengers.

review.arabic: إِذ نَجَّينـٰهُ وَأَهلَهُ أَجمَعينَ
review.meaning: Allah rescued Lūṭ and his family, according to the stated exceptions in surrounding verses.

review.arabic: ثُمَّ دَمَّرنَا الءاخَرينَ
review.meaning: The Qur’an recalls the destruction of the others after the rescue.

review.arabic: ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا لِلَّذينَ كَفَرُوا امرَأَتَ نوحٍ وَامرَأَتَ لوطٍ ۖ كانَتا تَحتَ عَبدَينِ مِن عِبادِنا صـٰلِحَينِ فَخانَتاهُما فَلَم يُغنِيا عَنهُما مِنَ اللَّهِ شَيـًٔا وَقيلَ ادخُلَا النّارَ مَعَ الدّٰخِلينَ
review.meaning: Allah uses the wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ as examples of people who betrayed faith while close to two righteous servants; closeness did not replace belief.

synthesis.text: The ten missions invite the child to understand a serious Prophetic account truthfully while developing habits of dignity, moral courage, care and responsibility. Prophet Lūṭ’s mission concerned worship and obedience to Allah and included clear warnings against serious sexual immorality and other corruption. Its conclusion teaches that Prophetic guidance is not measured by popular approval, and that Allah’s rescue and judgment occur by His will. These matters belong to revealed history; they must not be confused with the imagined events at an academy or in a family home.

The contemporary stories offer a narrower set of daily applications. We can learn to ask before sharing another person’s address or photograph. We can refuse to spread an unfair accusation. We can defend someone’s dignity through safe and lawful means. We can seek adult assistance when a child is threatened. We can keep promises, recognize that friendships do not excuse wrongdoing, and speak accurately about what revelation does and does not say. None of these activities purports to reproduce the extraordinary mission and suffering of a Prophet.

The world’s central message is that faithfulness to Allah should bring care and responsibility, never cruelty or sensationalism. A child’s value cannot be measured by their family background, a private struggle, or the choices of another person. Personal accountability is taught gently, with hope, privacy and room to learn.
Ten character values to carry forward
01. Respect the truth — Listen carefully to one person you usually overlook, then respond respectfully to what they actually say.
02. Choose right over popularity — Before sharing a photo or message today, check whether you have permission; if not, do not share it.
03. Protect the vulnerable — Notice one shared space today and help keep it safe and accessible for others.
04. Speak truth without abuse — Correct one small false statement kindly, using words that do not humiliate anyone.
05. Respect guests — Ask permission before taking or sharing a visitor’s photograph or personal details today.
06. Choose safe help — Identify one trustworthy adult you can go to for help if a child is threatened.
07. Own your decisions — Keep one small commitment or confidence you have been trusted with today.
08. Know when to seek safety — With a caregiver, identify the safest adult-help point at home or school.
09. Avoid careless judgments — Offer one simple kindness to someone facing difficulty, without asking them to explain their hardship.
10. Tell history faithfully — Check one religious or historical claim against a reliable source before repeating it.
Seven-day optional family practice journey
Day
One small, safe practice
Private check-in
Welcome a newcomer or younger learner respectfully.
Did my words help them feel safe?
Check before sharing any image, name or address.
Did I ask permission?
Make a shared corridor or play area safer for others.
Whose needs did I notice?
Correct a small false claim without insulting anyone.
Was my correction kind?
Keep one ordinary promise or confidence.
What helped me keep it?
Identify a trusted adult and a safe help-seeking step.
Do I know whom to contact?

The child may choose any days, skip a task, or ask a caregiver for an easier version. Do not reward reported personal sins, require photographs as proof, or punish missed days.
Final assessment — understanding without shame
Question
Teacher / developer expected answer
What was Prophet Lūṭ’s central religious duty?
Convey Allah’s message and call to obedience and righteousness.
Did the Qur’an address only poor hospitality?
No. It condemned grave sexual immorality and other wrongdoing, along with rejection of the Messenger.
Should a child physically confront a threatening crowd?
No. Seek safety and trusted-adult help.
Is it permissible to share a guest’s address without consent?
No.
Does 66:10 say Lūṭ’s wife committed adultery?
No. Classical explanation identifies betrayal in faith, not adultery.
Does a friendship or family tie replace your own responsibility?
No.
May a learner label a modern flood as divine punishment?
No; hidden divine judgments cannot be asserted without revelation.
Can children invent names, routes and speeches to make a Prophet’s story exciting?
No. Use authentic evidence and label uncertainties.
Can a wrong action become right because many people support it?
No.
What is one good habit you plan to practice?
Any safe, relevant habit such as protecting privacy, being truthful or asking for help.
